description: Inspired by information-theoretic branch-and-prune algorithms (Ahmed et al. 2023, used for RIS phase optimization), we propose applying information gain metrics to decide which branches of the Collatz bit-tree to explore first. Instead of DFS, use the 'dip' value (306k - 485f) as a heuristic priority: branches with higher dip values are more likely to be pruned by the bitvector lookahead, so explore low-dip branches first to find survivors quickly for GPU dispatch.
mathematical_formalization: Information gain of exploring branch b: IG(b) = H(survive|parent) - H(survive|parent, b), where H is entropy. Approximate: IG ≈ -log2(density(BV_{f-f_min})) for the corresponding bitvector. Priority queue: explore branches with highest expected survival first to minimize GPU idle time.
analogical_connections: Information-directed sampling in bandits — explore actions that maximize information about the optimum
A* search with admissible heuristic — use dip value as heuristic for distance to pruning
Huffman coding — assign shorter codes (less exploration) to more common events (more prunable branches)
implementation_hypothesis: Replace DFS in Algorithm 2 with a priority queue ordered by (f - f_min, current_dip). Process low-dip-high-f branches first, as they generate fewer GPU work items. Maintain a running count of dispatched GPU work items; when a batch of 2^16 is ready, launch a GPU kernel while continuing CPU-side tree exploration. This overlaps CPU recursion with GPU computation.
experiment_seed: Implement both DFS and priority-queue orderings for the recursive step. Measure: GPU utilization (fraction of time kernels are running), total wall-clock time, peak memory usage. Test on N=55 to compare with Angeltveit's reported 3636-second GPU time.
